claim: Neurons in primate V4 exhibit various types of selectivity for contour shapes, including curves, angles, and simple shapes.
source: Neurons in primate V4 exhibit various types of selectivity for contour shapes, including curves, angles, and simple shapes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about V4 neurons.

claim: Submillimeter functional domains exist in V4 that contain neurons preferring curved contours over rectilinear ones.
source: Using intrinsic signal optical imaging and two-photon calcium imaging, we observed submillimeter functional domains in V4 that contained neurons preferring curved contours over rectilinear ones.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ISOI and two-photon imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Curvature domains have similar sizes as orientation domains.
source: These curvature domains had similar sizes and response amplitudes as orientation domains but tended to separate from these regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2E comparing domain sizes.

claim: Curvature domains have similar response amplitudes as orientation domains.
source: These curvature domains had similar sizes and response amplitudes as orientation domains but tended to separate from these regions.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2F comparing response amplitudes.

claim: Curvature domains tend to separate from orientation domains.
source: These curvature domains had similar sizes and response amplitudes as orientation domains but tended to separate from these regions.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2G demonstrating less overlap than expected by chance.

claim: Within curvature domains, neurons that preferred circles or curve orientations clustered into finer scale subdomains.
source: Within the curvature domains, neurons that preferred circles or curve orientations clustered further into finer scale subdomains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Individual neurons have a wide range of contour selectivity.
source: Nevertheless, individual neurons also had a wide range of contour selectivity, and neighboring neurons exhibited a substantial diversity in shape tuning besides their common shape preferences.
evidence: This is shown by single-neuron response matrices in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Neighboring neurons exhibit substantial diversity in shape tuning besides their common shape preferences.
source: Nevertheless, individual neurons also had a wide range of contour selectivity, and neighboring neurons exhibited a substantial diversity in shape tuning besides their common shape preferences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the diversity of response patterns among neighboring neurons shown in Figure 7.

claim: V1 and V2 do not have contour-shape-related domains.
source: In strong contrast to V4, V1 and V2 did not have such contour-shape-related domains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D where circle vs. triangle patterns are absent in V1 and V2.

claim: V4 plays an important role in curvature processing.
source: These findings highlight the importance and complexity of curvature processing in visual object recognition and the key functional role of V4 in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of curvature domains in V4 but not V1/V2, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Shape extraction is crucial for object recognition.
source: Shape extraction is crucial for object recognition and is a major function of the primate visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Shape processing occurs in the ventral visual pathway (V1-V2-V4-IT) in a hierarchical manner.
source: This process has been reported to occur in the ventral visual pathway (V1-V2-V4-IT) in a hierarchical manner (Connor et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Connor et al., 2007.

claim: V4 plays an important role in shape processing.
source: The mid-level area V4 plays an important role in this process (Roe et al., 2012; Pasupathy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roe et al., 2012 and Pasupathy et al., 2020.

claim: Many V4 neurons selectively respond to curvatures.
source: Many V4 neurons selectively respond to curvatures (Pasupathy and Connor, 1999) and complex shape features (Desimone and Schein, 1987; Gallant et al., 1993; Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The distribution of shape-selective neurons in V4 remains unclear.
source: However, the distribution of these shape-selective neurons in V4 remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Orientation maps have been reported in V1, V2, and V4.
source: In the V1-V2-V4-IT pathway, orientation maps have been reported in V1, V2, and V4.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about functional organization in visual cortex.

claim: Functional maps for faces have been reported in IT.
source: Functional maps for faces (Wang et al., 1996; Tsao et al., 2006) and various shape features (Fujita et al., 1992; Tsunoda et al., 2001; Sato et al., 2009) have been reported in IT.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Functional maps for various shape features have been reported in IT.
source: Functional maps for faces (Wang et al., 1996; Tsao et al., 2006) and various shape features (Fujita et al., 1992; Tsunoda et al., 2001; Sato et al., 2009) have been reported in IT.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The processing hierarchy appears to lack functional structures for shape features of intermediate complexity, including curvatures and angles.
source: This processing hierarchy appears to lack functional structures for shape features of intermediate complexity, including curvatures and angles.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: A previous fMRI study reported several patches of the ventral cortex that prefer curved features with one being located in V4.
source: A previous fMRI study reported several patches of the ventral cortex that prefer curved features with one being located in V4 (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yue et al., 2014.

claim: The fMRI patches were relatively large (at the cm-scale) due to limited spatial resolution.
source: However, given the limited spatial resolution of fMRI signals, these patches were relatively large (at the cm-scale).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior fMRI studies.

claim: It remains unclear whether there are submillimeter functional columns for curvatures similar to those for edge orientations.
source: It remains unclear whether there are submillimeter functional columns for curvatures that are similar to those for edge orientations.
evidence: This is stated as the key question addressed by the current study.

claim: The exposed V4 region corresponded to the visual field of 0°−10° eccentricity in a lower quadrant.
source: The exposed V4 region corresponded to the visual field of 0°−10° eccentricity in a lower quadrant.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and visual field coverage.

claim: In the circle vs. triangle map, black and white patches corresponded to regions that preferred circles and triangles, respectively.
source: In the circle vs. triangle map (Figure 1D), the black and white patches corresponded to regions that preferred circles and triangles, respectively.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the functional maps shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The V4 pattern in circle vs. triangle map significantly differed from the orientation and color patterns.
source: This V4 pattern significantly differed from the orientation (Figure 1E) and color patterns (Figure 1F) obtained with established methods (Tanigawa et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing different functional maps in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Circle vs. triangle patterns were not observed in V1 and V2.
source: In contrast to V4, we did not observe circle vs. triangle patterns in V1 and V2, or in the cortex anterior to the superior temporal sulcus (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D where patterns are absent in V1 and V2.

claim: Circle vs. triangle patterns were not observed in the cortex anterior to the superior temporal sulcus.
source: In contrast to V4, we did not observe circle vs. triangle patterns in V1 and V2, or in the cortex anterior to the superior temporal sulcus (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The responses in single-condition maps were dominated by feature-non-specific activation.
source: We also examined single-condition maps (stimulus vs. blank); however, the responses were dominated by feature-non-specific activation and the shape-selective response patterns were not apparent (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 comparing single-condition and difference maps.

claim: Similar V4 patterns were observed in the circle vs. triangle, circle vs. line, and curve vs. line maps.
source: Similar V4 patterns were observed in the circle vs. triangle (Figure 1D), circle vs. line (Figure 1G), and curve vs. line maps (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the maps in Figures 1D, G, and H.

claim: The key contour feature responsible for the dark patches in curvature-related maps was the curviness.
source: This similarity suggests that the key contour feature responsible for these dark patches was the curviness.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of patterns across different curved stimuli.

claim: Curvature domains contain smaller substructures.
source: These curvature domains contained smaller substructures.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing curve-orientation maps.

claim: A map comparing differently oriented curves showed smaller and weaker patches within the curvature domains.
source: For example, a map comparing differently oriented curves showed smaller and weaker patches within the curvature domains (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the curve-orientation maps in Figure 1I.

claim: Curve orientation is different from grating orientation and has a range of 0–360°.
source: Note that this curve orientation (also called direction) is different from the grating orientation (0–180°) and has a range of 0–360°.
evidence: This is a clarification about the definition of curve orientation.

claim: Triangle-activated cortical regions appeared significantly weaker compared to curvature domains.
source: Compared with the curvature domains, triangle-activated cortical regions appeared significantly weaker.
evidence: This is observed in the triangle vs. line and angle vs. line maps in Figures 1J and K.

claim: Dark patches in triangle vs. line and angle vs. line maps were more diffused and weaker than those in circle vs. line or curve vs. line maps.
source: In the triangle vs. line (Figure 1J) and angle vs. line maps (Figure 1K), the dark patches (angle-preferring) were apparently more diffused and weaker than those in the circle vs. line or curve vs. line maps (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the maps in Figures 1G-K.

claim: The circle vs. triangle map had fewer and weaker white patches (triangle-preferring) than dark patches (circle-preferring).
source: This was also observed in the circle vs. triangle map (Figure 1D), which had fewer and weaker white patches (triangle-preferring) than dark patches (circle-preferring) (also see Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Orientation subdomains observed in the curve-orientation map were not present in the angle-orientation map.
source: Moreover, the orientation subdomains observed in the curve-orientation map (Figure 1I) were not present in the angle-orientation map (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figures 1I and 1L.

claim: Imaging results of seven hemispheres (cases) of six macaque monkeys were consistent.
source: Imaging results of seven hemispheres (cases) of six macaque monkeys were consistent (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the consistent patterns shown across multiple cases in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: Curvature domains were observed in the entire exposed V4 surface representing both foveal and peripheral visual fields.
source: We observed curvature domains in the entire exposed V4 surface representing both foveal and peripheral visual fields, but peripheral V4 tend to prefer larger circles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D with different circle sizes.

claim: Peripheral V4 tends to prefer larger circles.
source: We observed curvature domains in the entire exposed V4 surface representing both foveal and peripheral visual fields, but peripheral V4 tend to prefer larger circles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D showing eccentricity-dependent size preferences.

claim: Similar patterns can be repeatedly imaged from the same chamber over months.
source: Moreover, similar patterns can be repeatedly imaged from the same chamber over months (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 with maps from different dates.

claim: Modification of experimental conditions and noncritical stimulus parameters did not alter the main pattern features.
source: Modification of the experimental conditions (e.g. monocular left- or right-eye viewing conditions or binocular conditions, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2M and N) and noncritical stimulus parameters (e.g. contour brightness, filled disks, and regular vs. random contour arrangements) did not alter the main pattern features (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2M-N and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–I.

claim: The curvature domains had an average diameter of 518 ± 25 μm.
source: The curvature domains had an average diameter of 518 ± 25 μm (mean ± s.e.m), which was similar to that of the orientation domains (479 ± 16 μm, p=0.074, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the ISOI data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The orientation domains had an average diameter of 479 ± 16 μm.
source: The curvature domains had an average diameter of 518 ± 25 μm (mean ± s.e.m), which was similar to that of the orientation domains (479 ± 16 μm, p=0.074, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the ISOI data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The curvature domain size was not significantly different from orientation domain size (p=0.074).
source: The curvature domains had an average diameter of 518 ± 25 μm (mean ± s.e.m), which was similar to that of the orientation domains (479 ± 16 μm, p=0.074, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The curvature domains occupied 12.1 ± 1.7% of the V4 surface.
source: The curvature domains occupied 12.1 ± 1.7% of the V4 surface, smaller than the coverage of the orientation domains (22.3 ± 3.7%, p=0.025, paired t-test, n = 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the ISOI data.

claim: The orientation domains occupied 22.3 ± 3.7% of the V4 surface.
source: The curvature domains occupied 12.1 ± 1.7% of the V4 surface, smaller than the coverage of the orientation domains (22.3 ± 3.7%, p=0.025, paired t-test, n = 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the ISOI data.

claim: Curvature domain coverage was significantly smaller than orientation domain coverage (p=0.025).
source: The curvature domains occupied 12.1 ± 1.7% of the V4 surface, smaller than the coverage of the orientation domains (22.3 ± 3.7%, p=0.025, paired t-test, n = 7).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of coverage measurements.

claim: The intrinsic optical signal amplitude was numerically, but not significantly, larger for the circle vs. triangle maps than the orientation maps.
source: The intrinsic optical signal amplitude (percentage change), which was measured from the raw subtraction maps, was numerically, but not significantly, larger for the circle vs. triangle maps than the orientation maps (curvature domains: 0.036%, orientation domains: 0.029%, p=0.15, paired t-test, n = 7, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on measurements shown in Figure 2F with statistical comparison.

claim: Little overlap was observed between the curvature and orientation domains.
source: However, we observed little overlap between the curvature and orientation domains (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and quantified in Figure 2G.

claim: The overlap size between curvature and orientation domains was significantly smaller than expected in a random distribution (p=0.03).
source: The overlap size was significantly smaller than that expected in a random distribution (p=0.03, paired t-test, n = 7, Figure 2G), which indicates an avoidance tendency between both domains.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is an avoidance tendency between curvature and orientation domains.
source: The overlap size was significantly smaller than that expected in a random distribution (p=0.03, paired t-test, n = 7, Figure 2G), which indicates an avoidance tendency between both domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical analysis of overlap shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The curvature domains did not overlap with the color domains (p=0.004).
source: Moreover, the curvature domains did not overlap with the color domains (p=0.004, paired t-test, n = 7, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Triangle-preferring white patches tended to overlap with the orientation domains (p=0.003).
source: Contrastingly, the triangle-preferring white patches in the circle vs. triangle maps tended to overlap with the orientation (p=0.003, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) but not the color domains (p=0.17, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Triangle-preferring white patches did not overlap with color domains (p=0.17).
source: Contrastingly, the triangle-preferring white patches in the circle vs. triangle maps tended to overlap with the orientation (p=0.003, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) but not the color domains (p=0.17, paired t-test, n = 7; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ISOI used a metabolism-based hemodynamic signal.
source: ISOI used a metabolism-based hemodynamic signal; therefore, the actual neuronal responses and neuron constitution within these domains were unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of ISOI signals and their limitations.

claim: The actual neuronal responses and neuron constitution within curvature domains were unclear from ISOI alone.
source: ISOI used a metabolism-based hemodynamic signal; therefore, the actual neuronal responses and neuron constitution within these domains were unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of ISOI that motivated two-photon imaging.

claim: ISOI could not provide information regarding the variations in different cortical layers.
source: Moreover, ISOI could not provide information regarding the variations in different cortical layers.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of ISOI that motivated two-photon imaging.

claim: AAV1/9-GCaMP6s virus was injected into multiple locations in two chambers based on ISOI functional maps.
source: Based on the ISOI functional maps, we injected AAV1/9-GCaMP6s virus into multiple locations in two chambers (Cases 3 and 4 in Figure 2A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for two-photon imaging.

claim: The injections targeted either the centers of the curvature domains or regions outside these domains.
source: The injections targeted either the centers of the curvature domains or regions outside these domains.
evidence: This describes the targeting strategy for virus injections.

claim: The population receptive field of the imaged region was ~4° in size and approximately 7° from the fovea.
source: Mapped with both manual and computer-controlled visual stimuli, the population receptive field (RF) of this region was ~4° in size and approximately 7° from the fovea (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a measurement from the two-photon imaging experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Significant activation of neurons by circle stimuli was observed in the curvature domain.
source: Consistent with the ISOI results (Figure 3B), we observed significant activation of the neurons by circle stimuli (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in the two-photon calcium imaging data in Figure 3D.

claim: The whole frame showed a scaled-down response to triangles compared to circles.
source: The whole frame showed a scaled-down response to triangles (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in the two-photon calcium imaging data in Figure 3E.

claim: Different stimuli types mainly affected the population response amplitudes rather than activating different cells within the curvature domain.
source: The results demonstrate that different stimuli types mainly affected the population response amplitudes rather than activating different cells within the curvature domain.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing Figures 3D and 3E showing similar spatial patterns with different amplitudes.

claim: The imaged region showed a preference for curved over rectilinear stimuli.
source: This imaged region showed a preference for curved (red) over rectilinear (green) stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in the two-photon preference map in Figure 4B.

claim: Consistent preference patterns were observed for the two-photon map and the ISOI map from the same region.
source: Consistent preference patterns were observed for this two-photon map (Figure 4B) and the ISOI map from the same region (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Similar preference patterns were observed at deeper layers.
source: Similar preference patterns were observed at deeper layers for this (Figure 4B and C) and all five locations imaged at multiple depths (Figure 4D–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4B-I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 comparing different depths.

claim: The curvature domains form a columnar structure within at least the top V4 layers.
source: Therefore, the curvature domains form a columnar structure within at least the top V4 layers.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of preference patterns across depths shown in Figures 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Although neurons inside the domains exhibited a common preference for curve stimuli, individual neurons showed diverse response properties.
source: Although neurons inside the domains exhibited a common preference for curve stimuli, individual neurons showed diverse response properties.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the example neurons in Figure 3F showing different response patterns.

claim: Cell 2 was strongly activated by circle stimuli and also activated by multiple other stimuli.
source: Both neurons were strongly activated by circle stimuli; however, cell 2 was also activated by multiple other stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in the response traces in Figure 3F.

claim: Cell 3 showed strong responses to the triangle as well as a 45°-orientated line that resembled an edge of the triangle.
source: Cell 3 were selected from a region highly activated by rectilinear stimuli (Figure 4F arrow) and it showed strong responses to the triangle as well as a 45°-orientated line that resembled an edge of the triangle.
evidence: This is shown in the response traces in Figure 3F.

claim: Contour-tuning differences exist not only between cells belonging to different functional domains but also between cells within a functional domain.
source: Thus, at cellular level, contour-tuning differences exist not only between cells belonging to different functional domains but also between cells within a functional domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of responses shown in Figures 3F and further explored in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: There was a significant correlation between two-photon fluorescent responses and ISOI hemodynamic responses (Pearson r = 0.42, p=9.45×10−83).
source: There was a significant correlation between the two types of responses (Pearson r = 0.42, p=9.45×10−83, n = 1923).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4J with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant correlation between fluorescent responses to curves vs. lines and ISOI responses to circles vs. triangles (Pearson r = 0.43, p=9.35×10−88).
source: Similar to J, there was a significant correlation between the fluorescent responses (optimal orientation) to curves vs. lines and ISOI responses to circles vs. triangles (Pearson r = 0.43, p=9.35×10−88, n = 1923).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4K with statistical analysis.

claim: Neurons' RF sizes had a negative correlation with the circle-triangle preferential responses in ISOI imaging.
source: The RF sizes of all neurons measured (Y-axis) had a negative correlation with the circle-triangle preferential responses of the corresponding pixels in the ISOI imaging (X-axis, same as the X-axis values in J and K).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The average RF size was smaller for neurons inside the curvature domains (1.95 ± 0.032°) than those outside (2.37 ± 0.038°, p=1.15×10−14).
source: The average RF size was smaller for neurons inside the curvature domains (1.95 ± 0.032°, n = 583) than those outside (2.37 ± 0.038°, n = 835, p=1.15×10−14, t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4M with statistical comparison.

claim: Neurons with a stronger response to curved stimuli tended to have smaller RFs.
source: Overall, the neurons with a stronger response to curved stimuli tended to have smaller RFs (Figure 4L and M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-E) and greater surround suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G), which is consistent with previous findings on the relationship between end-stopping properties and curvature selectivity (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Dobbins et al., 1987; Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4L-M and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-E, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Neurons with a stronger response to curved stimuli tended to have greater surround suppression.
source: Overall, the neurons with a stronger response to curved stimuli tended to have smaller RFs (Figure 4L and M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-E) and greater surround suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G), which is consistent with previous findings on the relationship between end-stopping properties and curvature selectivity (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Dobbins et al., 1987; Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-G and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The relationship between RF size/surround suppression and curvature preference is consistent with previous findings on end-stopping properties and curvature selectivity.
source: Overall, the neurons with a stronger response to curved stimuli tended to have smaller RFs (Figure 4L and M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-E) and greater surround suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G), which is consistent with previous findings on the relationship between end-stopping properties and curvature selectivity (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Dobbins et al., 1987; Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Dobbins et al., 1987; Ponce et al., 2017.

claim: Curvature domains imaged with curves and circles in ISOI were generally similar.
source: Curvature domains imaged with curves and circles in ISOI were generally similar (e.g. Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figures 1G and H.

claim: Individual neurons inside the curvature domain often showed different responses to curves and circles.
source: However, individual neurons inside the curvature domain often showed different responses to these two stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the example neurons in Figure 6A-F showing different preferences.

claim: Among the 788 neurons imaged inside the curvature domains, circle-preferring comprised 25.6% (202).
source: Among the 788 neurons imaged inside the curvature domains, circle-preferring comprised 25.6% (202), dual-preference comprised 14.4% (113), and curve-orientation-preferring neurons comprised 19.2% (151), with the rest not passing the statistical tests.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neuron types from two-photon imaging data.

claim: Among the 788 neurons imaged inside the curvature domains, dual-preference comprised 14.4% (113).
source: Among the 788 neurons imaged inside the curvature domains, circle-preferring comprised 25.6% (202), dual-preference comprised 14.4% (113), and curve-orientation-preferring neurons comprised 19.2% (151), with the rest not passing the statistical tests.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neuron types from two-photon imaging data.

claim: Among the 788 neurons imaged inside the curvature domains, curve-orientation-preferring neurons comprised 19.2% (151).
source: Among the 788 neurons imaged inside the curvature domains, circle-preferring comprised 25.6% (202), dual-preference comprised 14.4% (113), and curve-orientation-preferring neurons comprised 19.2% (151), with the rest not passing the statistical tests.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neuron types from two-photon imaging data.

claim: Among the 1135 neurons outside the curvature domains, circle-preferring comprised 7.3% (83).
source: The corresponding proportions of these three groups in the 1135 neurons outside the curvature domains were 7.3% (83), 1.8% (20), and 11.7% (133), respectively (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neuron types from two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Among the 1135 neurons outside the curvature domains, dual-preference comprised 1.8% (20).
source: The corresponding proportions of these three groups in the 1135 neurons outside the curvature domains were 7.3% (83), 1.8% (20), and 11.7% (133), respectively (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neuron types from two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Among the 1135 neurons outside the curvature domains, curve-orientation-preferring neurons comprised 11.7% (133).
source: The corresponding proportions of these three groups in the 1135 neurons outside the curvature domains were 7.3% (83), 1.8% (20), and 11.7% (133), respectively (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of neuron types from two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The summed proportion of the three types of neurons was larger inside the curvature domains (59.1%) than outside (20.8%).
source: As expected, the summed proportion of these three types of neurons was larger inside the curvature domains (59.1%) than the outside (20.8%).
evidence: This is calculated from the proportions reported for neurons inside and outside curvature domains.

claim: The ratio of circle-preferring to curve-orientation-preferring neurons appeared to be larger inside (1.35) than outside (0.62) the curvature domains.
source: The ratio of circle-preferring to curve-orientation-preferring neurons also appeared to be larger inside (1.35) than outside (0.62) the curvature domains.
evidence: This is calculated from the proportions of different neuron types.

claim: There was a tendency of spatial clustering of neurons according to their types.
source: When neurons were labeled according to their preferences, there was a tendency of spatial clustering according to their types (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G where neurons of similar types are spatially grouped.

claim: Curve-orientation-preferring neurons further clustered based on their preferred orientations.
source: Moreover, the curve-orientation-preferring neurons further clustered based on their preferred orientations (Figure 6H), which is consistent with the ISOI results (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H and is consistent with ISOI results in Figure 1I.

claim: The average distances for within-group neuron pairs were shorter than the average distance between two randomly selected neurons.
source: The average distances for within-group neuron pairs were shorter than the average distance between two randomly selected neurons (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6J demonstrating spatial clustering.

claim: The size of curve-orientation subdomain was around 360 μm.
source: Periodicity analysis shows the size of curve-orientation subdomain was around 360 μm (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 from periodicity analysis.

claim: For circle-preferring neurons, their responses increased approximately linearly with the length of the circle fragment.
source: For circle-preferring neurons, their responses increased approximately linearly with the length of the circle fragment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6K plotting responses to different contours.

claim: Circle-preferring neurons' responses to closed shapes seemed to be proportional to the general similarity between the shape and the circle.
source: Also, their responses to closed shapes seemed to be proportional to the general similarity between the shape and the circle.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6K plotting responses to different shapes.

claim: For neighboring neurons, although their general shape preferences were similar, their contour response patterns still vary from cell to cell.
source: Thus, for neighboring neurons, although their general shape preferences were similar, which constitute the basis of the ISOI signals, their contour response patterns still vary from cell to cell, and some of the differences were substantial.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the diversity of response matrices shown in Figure 7.

claim: Some of the differences in contour response patterns among neighboring neurons were substantial.
source: Thus, for neighboring neurons, although their general shape preferences were similar, which constitute the basis of the ISOI signals, their contour response patterns still vary from cell to cell, and some of the differences were substantial.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the diversity of response matrices shown in Figure 7.

claim: The degrees of diversity in contour tuning seem to be related to the types of sites in V4.
source: The degrees of such diversity also seem to be related to the types of these sites in V4.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the diversity patterns across different site types shown in Figure 7.

claim: Curvature neurons showed much higher response amplitudes than neurons in rectilinear domains or outside both domain types.
source: In the orientation-sorted average response matrices, curvature neurons showed much higher response amplitudes, and larger differences between curved and rectilinear responses, than the other two types of neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A-C comparing average response matrices.

claim: Curvature neurons showed larger differences between curved and rectilinear responses than neurons in rectilinear domains or outside both domain types.
source: In the orientation-sorted average response matrices, curvature neurons showed much higher response amplitudes, and larger differences between curved and rectilinear responses, than the other two types of neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A-C comparing average response matrices.

claim: Curvature neurons also responded to rectilinear stimuli at about half of the response amplitude.
source: Nevertheless, these neurons also responded to rectilinear stimuli, for example the triangles, at about half of the response amplitude.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A comparing responses to different stimuli.

claim: Neurons in rectilinear domains did not show prominent differences in their responses to rectilinear and curved stimuli.
source: Interestingly, neurons in rectilinear domains did not show prominent differences in their responses to rectilinear and curved stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The weak differentiation in rectilinear domains is consistent with the weak rectilinear domains in ISOI imaging.
source: This is also consistent with the weak rectilinear domains in ISOI imaging (Figure 1D).
evidence: This connects the two-photon findings with the ISOI observations in Figure 1D.

claim: A novel functional structure in V4 for curved contour processing was found using two complementary imaging methods.
source: Using two complementary imaging methods, we found a novel functional structure in V4, but not in V1 or V2, for curved contour processing.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study based on ISOI and two-photon imaging.

claim: The size of curvature domains (518 µm) was similar to that of the orientation domains in V4.
source: The size of these domains (518 µm) was similar to that of the orientation domains in this area; moreover, they tended to occupy regions outside the orientation domains.
evidence: This is based on measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Curvature domains tended to occupy regions outside the orientation domains.
source: The size of these domains (518 µm) was similar to that of the orientation domains in this area; moreover, they tended to occupy regions outside the orientation domains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and quantified in Figure 2G.

claim: Within curvature domains, neurons preferring different curve features further clustered into smaller subdomains.
source: Within these domains, neurons preferring different curve features (e.g. curve orientation) further clustered into smaller subdomains.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6G and H.

claim: Subdomains were also found in color-, orientation-, and direction-specific regions in V4.
source: Interestingly, subdomains were also found in color- (Li et al., 2014; Ghose and Ts'o, 2017; Liu et al., 2020), orientation- (Ghose and Ts'o, 1997; Tanigawa et al., 2010), and direction- (Li et al., 2013) specific regions in V4.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: These nested functional architectures are similar to that of category domains in IT.
source: These nested functional architectures are similar to that of category domains in IT, where large category domains (animate vs. inanimate) contain subcategory domains (e.g. for face and body parts) (Liu et al., 2013; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013 and Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014.

claim: Curvature domains are probably vertical columns.
source: Curvature domains are probably vertical columns.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of preferences across depths shown in Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual neurons usually responded to a wide range of stimuli with different levels of response amplitudes.
source: First, individual neurons usually responded to a wide range of stimuli with different levels of response amplitudes.
evidence: This is shown in the response matrices in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Curvature domains are not 'curvature-only' domains.
source: Thus, curvature domains are not 'curvature-only' domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neurons in curvature domains also respond to non-curved stimuli.

claim: Neurons inside the curvature domains and those outside do not completely differ in their stimulus coverage, although their optimal stimuli are usually different.
source: Second, neurons inside the curvature domains and those outside do not completely differ in their stimulus coverage, although their optimal stimuli are usually different.
evidence: This is shown by comparing response patterns in Figure 8A-C.

claim: For neighboring neurons within a functional domain, although they showed common shape preferences, many of them exhibited different individual preferences, some of which were substantial.
source: Third, for neighboring neurons within a functional domain, although they showed common shape preferences, many of them exhibited different individual preferences, some of which were substantial.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the diversity of responses shown in Figure 7.

claim: The functional maps observed are best understood as a certain orderness of the complexity of shape responses in V4 population.
source: Thus, the functional maps we observed are best understood as a certain orderness of the complexity of shape responses in V4 population.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the findings based on the observed complexity and diversity.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous findings that V4 plays a key functional role in the representation and processing of curvature information.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Pasupathy and Connor, 1999; Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; Pasupathy and Connor, 2002; Yue et al., 2014), we confirmed that V4 plays a key functional role in the representation and processing of curvature information.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and the current findings.

claim: A majority of V4 neurons have been reported to exhibit complex multi-dimensional response patterns to shape stimuli.
source: A majority of V4 neurons have been reported to exhibit complex multi-dimensional response patterns to shape stimuli (Gallant et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gallant et al., 1993.

claim: Recent studies in V4 and IT have shown that individual neurons can be best activated by non-natural synthetic patterns that are much more complex than those traditionally tested.
source: Recent studies in V4 (Bashivan et al., 2019) and IT (Ponce et al., 2019) have shown that individual neurons in these areas can be best activated by non-natural synthetic patterns that are much more complex than those traditionally tested.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bashivan et al., 2019 and Ponce et al., 2019.

claim: Classifying neurons into functionally separate groups based on their contour responses is often difficult.
source: Thus, classifying neurons into functionally separate groups based on their contour responses is often difficult.
evidence: This is stated as a general challenge in the field based on the complexity of neuronal responses.

claim: Intrinsic functional structures in an area are suggestive of particular feature dimensions been emphasized in this area.
source: However, intrinsic functional structures in an area are suggestive of particular feature dimensions been emphasized in this area.
evidence: This is a general principle about the significance of functional organization.

claim: V4 contains clear maps for curvature processing, which suggests that curvature is a unique feature dimension in this area.
source: We observed that V4 contains clear maps for curvature processing, which suggests that curvature is a unique feature dimension in this area, not only in single neurons but also as a populational feature.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of curvature domains shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both curved and rectilinear contours formed functional structures with each containing nested subdomains for further detailed tuning.
source: Further, both curved and rectilinear contours formed functional structures (curvature and orientation domains) with each functional structure containing nested subdomains for further detailed tuning (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6G and H.

claim: This functional organization could underlie the parallel processing of curved and straight contours.
source: This functional organization could underlie the parallel processing of curved and straight contours (Ito, 2012) and the different underlying pooling mechanisms (Nandy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on the functional organization observed and supported by citations to Ito, 2012 and Nandy et al., 2013.

claim: In human fMRI studies, V4 is more activated by circular stimulus than by curves or parallel patterns.
source: In human fMRI studies, V4 is more activated by circular stimulus than by curves (Dumoulin and Hess, 2007) or parallel patterns (Wilkinson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dumoulin and Hess, 2007 and Wilkinson et al., 2000.

claim: Many circle-preferring neurons were observed using two-photon imaging.
source: Using two-photon imaging, we observed many circle-preferring neurons (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I with quantification of neuron types.

claim: Circle-preferring neurons also showed good responses to other non-circle stimuli.
source: However, these circle-preferring neurons also showed good responses to other non-circle stimuli (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Many curve-orientation-preferring neurons also responded best to circles.
source: Many curve-orientation-preferring neurons also responded best to circles (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C for dual-preference neurons.

claim: Circle-preferring neurons do not constitute a functionally distinct subdivision of V4.
source: This indicates that these circle-preferring neurons do not constitute a functionally distinct subdivision of V4.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap in response properties between circle-preferring and other neurons.

claim: Early single-cell recordings have suggested that V4 neurons may cluster based on their color or orientation preferences.
source: Early single-cell recordings have suggested that V4 neurons may cluster based on their color or orientation preferences (e.g. Tanaka et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 1986.

claim: Subsequent optical imaging studies confirmed functional structures for color and orientation in V4.
source: Subsequent optical imaging studies confirmed these functional structures (Ghose and Ts'o, 1997; Tanigawa et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple optical imaging studies.

claim: Clustering of shape-responsive neurons according to their selectivity to complex patterns has been suggested.
source: For shape-responsive neurons, clustering according to their selectivity to complex patterns has also been suggested (Tanaka et al., 1986; Gallant et al., 1993; Gallant et al., 1996), but studies have also shown that neurons selective to complex shape features are mixed with those selective to simple features such as orientations (Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Studies have shown that neurons selective to complex shape features are mixed with those selective to simple features such as orientations.
source: For shape-responsive neurons, clustering according to their selectivity to complex patterns has also been suggested (Tanaka et al., 1986; Gallant et al., 1993; Gallant et al., 1996), but studies have also shown that neurons selective to complex shape features are mixed with those selective to simple features such as orientations (Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994.

claim: Although neurons tended to cluster according to their common response preferences, substantial diversity in contour tuning still exists among these clustered neurons.
source: Our results confirmed that, although neurons tended to cluster according to their common response preferences, substantial diversity in contour tuning still exist among these clustered neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the diversity shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Heterogeneity in neuronal responses may make functional organizations less detectable in electrophysiological studies compared to orientation columns in V1.
source: This heterogeneity may make these functional organizations less detectable in electrophysiological studies, for example, compared to the orientation columns in V1.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed heterogeneity and comparison with V1.

claim: Jiang et al., 2019 imaged cellular responses in parafoveal V4 representations to a large set of natural and artificial stimuli.
source: In a recent two-photon calcium imaging study posted on bioRxiv, Jiang et al., 2019 imaged cellular responses in parafoveal V4 representations (~1° eccentricity from the fovea) to a large set of natural and artificial stimuli.
evidence: This is a citation to a related study.

claim: Jiang et al., 2019 findings suggested a separate coding for orientation, curve and angle.
source: Their findings suggested a separate coding for orientation, curve and angle.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Jiang et al., 2019.

claim: Due to spatial limitation of two-photon technique, domain features and distributions are not available in Jiang et al., 2019.
source: However, due to the spatial limitation of the two-photon technique, domain features and distributions are not available.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Jiang et al., 2019 study.

claim: With ISOI over a large imaging window, the distribution of curvature domains and their spatial relationships with other functional maps were observed.
source: With ISOI over a large imaging window (16–20 mm diameter), we observed the distribution of the curvature domains and their spatial relationships with other known functional maps (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Curvature domains existed in the entire exposed V4 surface (0–10° eccentricity from the fovea).
source: We found that curvature domains existed in the entire exposed V4 surface (0–10° eccentricity from the fovea).
evidence: This is shown across multiple cases in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: The ISOI maps of the curvature and orientation domains were comparable, suggesting they had a comparable degree of clustering.
source: Further, the ISOI maps of the curvature and orientation domains were comparable (Figure 2F), which suggests that they had a comparable degree of clustering.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F comparing map strengths.

claim: Hu et al., 2020 investigated curvature organization in area V4 with ISOI and observed curvature domains similar to what was observed in this study.
source: In another study also submitted to eLife, Hu et al., 2020 investigated curvature organization in area V4 with ISOI. Despite a different stimulus protocol they used, they observed curvature domains similar to what we observed.
evidence: This is a citation to a related concurrent study.

claim: The major ISOI findings are similar between Hu et al., 2020 and this study.
source: The major ISOI findings are similar between these two studies.
evidence: This is a comparison with the Hu et al., 2020 study.

claim: With two-photon imaging, this study not only confirmed ISOI findings but also revealed neuronal properties underlying these domains.
source: With the power of two-photon imaging, we not only confirmed these ISOI findings but also revealed neuronal properties underlying these domains, including cellular-level preferences and the tuning diversity of neurons within these functional domains.
evidence: This is a summary of the contributions of the current study.

claim: Hu et al., 2020 and this study both revealed the overall features of curvature domains in V4.
source: Thus, Hu et al., 2020 and this study both revealed the overall features of curvature domains in V4, while Jiang et al., 2019 and this study both revealed cellular-level features of the functional domains.
evidence: This is a comparison of the contributions of different studies.

claim: Jiang et al., 2019 and this study both revealed cellular-level features of the functional domains.
source: Thus, Hu et al., 2020 and this study both revealed the overall features of curvature domains in V4, while Jiang et al., 2019 and this study both revealed cellular-level features of the functional domains.
evidence: This is a comparison of the contributions of different studies.

claim: Only this study directly linked functional domain properties with their underlining neural responses.
source: Only this study directly linked functional domain properties with their underlining neural responses.
evidence: This is stated as a unique contribution of the current study.

claim: Curve-preferring neurons have been reported in V1, V2, and V4.
source: Curve-preferring neurons have been reported in V1, V2, and V4 (Hegdé and Van Essen, 2007; Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hegdé and Van Essen, 2007 and Ponce et al., 2017.

claim: Functional structures for curves were not observed in V1 and V2.
source: However, we did not observe functional structures for curves in V1 and V2, which is consistent with a previous study (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with Yue et al., 2014.

claim: Curvature domains emerge in V4 and remain present in IT.
source: Curvature domains emerge in V4 (Yue et al., 2014; this study) and remain present in IT (Yue et al., 2014; Srihasam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and the current findings.

claim: V4 contains both basic orientation maps (similar to V1 and V2) and curvature maps (similar to IT).
source: Therefore, V4 contains both basic orientation (similar to V1 and V2) and curvature maps (similar to IT), which indicates its intermediate-stage role in the shape processing hierarchy.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of both types of maps shown in the study.

claim: V4's functional organization indicates its intermediate-stage role in the shape processing hierarchy.
source: Therefore, V4 contains both basic orientation (similar to V1 and V2) and curvature maps (similar to IT), which indicates its intermediate-stage role in the shape processing hierarchy.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of features observed in V4.

claim: There is a progressive change in multiple feature dimensions along the V1-V2-V4-IT hierarchy.
source: There is a progressive change in multiple feature dimensions along this hierarchy, for example receptive field size, response linearity, and degree of modulation by top-down controls.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the visual processing hierarchy.

claim: Functional architectures for shape processing form an independent dimension that could contribute to understanding neural mechanisms for shape processing.
source: Functional architectures for shape processing form an independent dimension, which could contribute to a better understanding of the neural mechanisms for shape processing.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: The consistency between functional architectures and shape processing levels highlights the importance of functional organization in the brain.
source: Moreover, the consistency between functional architectures and shape processing levels highlights the importance of functional organization in the brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the correspondence between functional organization and processing hierarchy.

claim: This study provides another measurement type (domain-level activation) for studies on shape processing in addition to cellular- and voxel-level measurements.
source: This study provides another measurement type (domain-level activation) for studies on shape processing in addition to the cellular- and voxel-level measurements.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: Curvature neurons had smaller RFs than those of non-curvature neurons.
source: We have shown that curvature neurons had smaller RFs than those of non-curvature neurons (Figure 4L and M).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4L and M.

claim: Curvature neurons had stronger surround suppression.
source: We further analyzed and showed that curvature neurons had stronger surround suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Curvature neurons exhibited end-stopping properties consistent with previous findings.
source: Thus, consistent with previous findings, curvature neurons did exhibit end-stopping properties.
evidence: This is consistent with prior literature on end-stopping and curvature selectivity.

claim: Curvature neurons showed additional curve-specific preferences beyond end-stopping properties.
source: However, curvature neurons showed additional curve-specific preferences, including curve-orientation tuning, preference for curves over similarly-sized angle stimuli, etc.
evidence: This is shown in the detailed analysis of curvature neuron responses in Figure 6.

claim: Circle-preferring neurons prefer circles (larger) than the half-circles (smaller).
source: For circle-preferring neurons, they prefer circles (larger) than the half-circles (smaller).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Additional features suggest that curvature neurons were not simple end-stopping neurons, although they exhibited end-stopping properties.
source: These additional features suggest that curvature neurons were not simple end-stopping neurons, although they exhibited end-stopping properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of end-stopping and curve-specific properties.

claim: Curvature domains are unlikely the suppression-domains (S-domains) in V4 revealed by comparing activations to small and large patches of gratings.
source: Curvature domains are also unlikely the suppression-domains (S-domains) in V4 revealed by comparing activations to small and large patches of gratings (Ghose and Ts'o, 1997).
evidence: This is argued based on the stimulus design and comparison with prior work.

claim: In curvature domain difference maps, the two stimuli in each pair had similar sizes and thus had similar surround suppression effects.
source: In our study, curvature domains were revealed in difference maps, including: circles vs. triangles (Figure 1D), circles vs. bars (Figure 1G), curves vs. bars (Figure 1H), and curves vs. angles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2L). The two stimuli in each pair had similar sizes, and thus had similar surround suppression effects.
evidence: This is stated as part of the argument that curvature domains are not suppression domains.

claim: The contrast pattern in curvature domain difference maps could not be due to differences in suppression.
source: Their contrast pattern in the difference maps could not be due to differences in suppression.
evidence: This is argued based on the matched stimulus sizes.

claim: The stimuli in curvature domain difference maps had balanced orientations and their maps had little overlap with the orientation maps.
source: The stimuli on the two sides also had balanced orientations, plus their maps had little overlap with the orientation maps (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and is part of the argument against orientation-based explanations.

claim: The only consistent contrast in the stimulus pairs for curvature domains was the curvature feature.
source: The only consistent contrasts in these pairs of stimuli was the curvature feature.
evidence: This is argued based on analysis of the stimulus properties.

claim: The curvature domains found are unlikely related to suppression and orientation domains.
source: Thus, the curvature domains we found are unlikely related to suppression and orientation domains.
evidence: This is concluded based on the arguments about stimulus design and domain overlap.

claim: Two-photon results have limitations in terms of the stimulus set, anesthetized preparation, and calcium signals.
source: Our two-photon results have limitations in terms of the stimulus set, anesthetized preparation, and calcium signals.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Only 19 simple contour shapes were tested, mostly with four orientations.
source: We only tested 19 simple contour shapes, mostly with four orientations.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the stimulus set.

claim: Considering the complexity of single-cell response patterns observed, the best-driven stimuli identified may not be the optimal ones for the neurons.
source: Considering the complexity of single-cell response patterns we observed, the best-driven stimuli we identified may not be the optimal ones for the neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and caveat about the findings.

claim: A deep-learning-network approach successfully found optimal stimuli for V4 neurons.
source: A recently reported deep-learning-network approach successfully found optimal stimuli for V4 neurons (Bashivan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bashivan et al., 2019.

claim: The optimal stimuli found by deep-learning approach were usually complex patterns and unlike the contour shapes previously tested.
source: The optimal stimuli they found were usually complex patterns and unlike the contour shapes previously tested.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Bashivan et al., 2019.

claim: The optimal stimulus patterns from deep-learning also contained specific curvature features similar to the optimal ones obtained with a parametric stimulus set.
source: However, these optimal stimulus patterns also contained specific curvature features similar to the optimal ones obtained with a parametric stimulus set like ours.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with Bashivan et al., 2019 findings.

claim: It is likely that the best-driven contour features obtained should also be represented in the actual optimal stimuli for the neurons measured.
source: Thus, it is likely that the best-driven contour features we obtained should also be represented in the actual optimal stimuli for the neurons we measured.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with deep-learning findings.

claim: ISOI tests provided a practical way in designing and narrowing down the stimulus set for the subsequent targeted two-photon imaging.
source: Our ISOI tests also provided a practical way in designing and narrowing down the stimulus set for the subsequent targeted two-photon imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The primary new finding of this study is the functional architecture for curvature processing in V4.
source: The primary new finding of this study is the functional architecture for curvature processing in V4.
evidence: This is stated as the main contribution of the study.

claim: The curvature domain likely shares similar formational rules and functional significances with other functional architectures previously discovered.
source: The curvature domain likely shares similar formational rules and functional significances with other functional architectures previously discovered (Mountcastle, 1997; Chklovskii and Koulakov, 2004).
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with other functional architectures and supported by citations.

claim: The relative separation of the curvature and rectilinear domains suggests a parallel processing of these two contour features.
source: For example, the relative separation of the curvature and rectilinear domains suggests a parallel processing of these two contour features.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial separation shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: The existence of the circle and curve-orientation sub-domains within the curvature domains suggests that there are different processes for curvatures.
source: The existence of the circle and curve-orientation sub-domains within the curvature domains suggests that there are different processes for curvatures.
evidence: This is inferred from the subdomains shown in Figures 6G and H.

claim: The existence of curvature domains provides an efficient way to study curvature neurons in V4.
source: Finally, the existence of curvature domains also provides an efficient way to study curvature neurons in V4, for example, by targeted recording, imaging, or tracer labeling.
evidence: This is stated as a practical implication of the findings.

claim: A total of seven hemispheres (cases) from six adult male macaque monkeys were imaged.
source: A total of seven hemispheres (i.e. cases) from six adult male macaque monkeys (five Macaca mulatta, one Macaca fascicularis) were imaged.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: ISOI were performed on all seven cases.
source: ISOI were performed on all seven cases, two-photon imaging were performed on two cases (Case 3 and Case 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedures.

claim: Two-photon imaging were performed on two cases (Case 3 and Case 4).
source: ISOI were performed on all seven cases, two-photon imaging were performed on two cases (Case 3 and Case 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedures.

claim: All procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Beijing Normal University.
source: All procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Beijing Normal University (protocol number: IACUC(BNU)-NKCNL2016-06).
evidence: This is stated as part of the ethical compliance of the study.
